static.whatIsIt: Starlink is SpaceX’s low-Earth-orbit satellite internet constellation, delivering broadband through thousands of small satellites. Its terminals have been used in Ukraine for civilian and military communications since the 2022 Russian invasion.
static.background: SpaceX began deploying Starlink satellites in 2019 and opened service in Ukraine after Russia’s 2022 invasion. Ukraine’s reliance on the network made a commercial firm a key node in battlefield communications, raising questions about private control over strategic infrastructure.
static.geography: Low Earth orbit, global coverage; the Ukraine war theatre is a key use case.
static.socioEconomic: Demonstrates states’ dependence on private dual-use infrastructure; commercial decisions can affect military operations and civilian connectivity.
static.whyInNews: Democratic U.S. senators have sought preservation of records on Musk’s and SpaceX’s handling of Starlink access in Ukraine.
static.wayForward: States should develop clear frameworks for contracting, contingency back-ups, data retention and oversight of commercial dual-use space services; international norms on private actors in conflict need clarity.

static.topic: US Congressional Oversight and Preservation of Records
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Functions of legislatures; legislative oversight and accountability
static.whatIsIt: In the U.S. system, congressional committees investigate executive and private-sector conduct, seek documents and may issue preservation letters before formal subpoenas. Such demands are part of legislative oversight, not a judicial order.
static.background: Congress’s investigative power derives from its constitutional legislative role; committees have historically sought records in probes ranging from war powers to government contracts. A preservation letter asks recipients not to destroy relevant material while oversight proceeds.
static.socioEconomic: Oversight of public contracts and private contractors affects transparency and democratic accountability.
static.whyInNews: Senators moved to preserve records on Starlink’s Ukraine access, a precursor to possible formal congressional scrutiny.
static.wayForward: Legislatures should pair preservation demands with clear timelines, scope and legal process to balance oversight with due process and commercial confidentiality.
prelimsPointers: A congressional preservation letter is not itself a subpoena; it demands that relevant records not be destroyed.
U.S. congressional committees can investigate matters within their legislative jurisdiction.
Legislative oversight is a check on both executive agencies and private contractors.

stories.headline: Voter Roll Deletions, Housing Fraud and Agnipath Row Stir Governance Debate
stories.summary: Ahead of assembly elections, political parties and the Election Commission are locked in a dispute over the accuracy of electoral rolls. In Uttar Pradesh, the BJP has set a target of restoring 'deleted' Hindu voters, framing it as a final opportunity ('antim mauka'), while in West Bengal an analysis of 22 constituencies found nearly 30,000 electors still 'under adjudication' against the Commission's statewide figure of about 6,000. Separately, the West Bengal Chief Minister flagged around 12,000 'fake' housing beneficiaries and ordered recovery of funds and departmental probes into officials. Meanwhile, a critical op-ed on the Agnipath scheme argued that senior military leadership failed to voice reservations about the short-service recruitment model.
stories.whyItMatters: The row tests the credibility of the ECI's roll-revision machinery and the accountability of welfare delivery — both recurring GS-II governance themes — while the Agnipath debate feeds directly into GS-III defence reform.

perspectives.take: Reports the BJP's Uttar Pradesh unit setting a 'last chance' target to restore deleted Hindu voters, framing roll revision as a state-level political mobilisation exercise ahead of assembly polls.

static.topic: Election Commission of India and Electoral Roll Revision
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Constitutional Bodies; Elections and Electoral Reforms
static.whatIsIt: The ECI is a constitutional body under Article 324 vested with the superintendence, direction and control of elections; electoral rolls are prepared and revised under the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
static.background: The Commission was set up on 25 January 1950 (observed as National Voters' Day) and became a multi-member body in 1993 with two Election Commissioners. Rolls are revised annually through Special Summary Revision, involving draft publication, a claims-and-objections window and final publication. Deletions follow verification of death, permanent shift, duplicate entries or electors not traceable.
static.geography: West Bengal (294 assembly seats) and Uttar Pradesh (403 assembly seats) — the two states in the news.
static.socioEconomic: Deletions disproportionately affect poor and migrant electors who may lack documentary proof of residence, shifting the burden of proving eligibility onto the voter.
static.whyInNews: The UP BJP's 'antim mauka' target for restoring deleted voters, and The Wire's finding of nearly 30,000 electors 'under adjudication' in 22 Bengal seats against the ECI's statewide figure of about 6,000.
static.wayForward: Publish auditable deletion lists with reasoned orders, expand ERONET-based digital claims and objections, and use SVEEP outreach so vulnerable electors can re-establish eligibility before polls.
prelimsPointers: ECI is a constitutional body under Article 324; it became a multi-member body in 1993.
Electoral rolls are prepared under the RP Act, 1950, while the RP Act, 1951 governs conduct of elections and election disputes.
National Voters' Day is observed on 25 January.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether the ECI's roll-revision process adequately balances purity of the electoral roll with the right of every eligible citizen to vote, and suggest procedural safeguards.

static.topic: Agnipath Scheme and Defence Recruitment Reform
static.syllabusNode: Security — Defence Forces, Recruitment and Government Policies
static.whatIsIt: A short-service recruitment scheme announced in June 2022 for personnel below officer rank in the Army, Navy and Air Force, with a four-year engagement and retention of 25% in the regular cadre.
static.background: Introduced to lower the average age profile and the pension bill of the armed forces. Agniveers receive a Seva Nidhi package on exit but are not entitled to pension or gratuity; the scheme triggered widespread protests in 2022 and was followed by announcements of reservation for Agniveers in some paramilitary and state police forces.
static.socioEconomic: The debate centres on job security, long-term pension liability and the attractiveness of military service for rural youth.
static.whyInNews: A critical op-ed argued that senior generals did not publicly voice their reservations about the scheme.
static.wayForward: Periodic parliamentary and internal review of retention rates, training quality and unit cohesion, along with clarity on post-service pathways for those not retained.
prelimsPointers: Agnipath was announced in June 2022; the engagement is four years with up to 25% retained in the regular cadre.
Agniveers receive a Seva Nidhi package on completion of service but no pension.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the strategic, financial and social implications of short-service recruitment for the Indian armed forces.

static.topic: Welfare Delivery, Beneficiary Verification and Audit
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Transparency, Accountability, E-governance and Welfare Schemes
static.whatIsIt: Centrally sponsored housing schemes such as Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana–Gramin (2016) and PMAY–Urban (2015) provide construction assistance; beneficiary lists are drawn from SECC 2011 and the Awaas+ app, with Aadhaar-seeded DBT and geo-tagged monitoring.
static.background: PMAY-G was launched with a 'Housing for All' target of about 2.95 crore rural houses, relying on Gram Sabha approval, social audit and state inspection. States have periodically reported ineligible or duplicate beneficiaries, leading to recovery proceedings against them.
static.geography: West Bengal — the state in the news; it has run a parallel state housing scheme amid disputes with the Centre over PMAY-G implementation.
static.socioEconomic: Housing assistance is a core poverty-alleviation instrument, so leakages and wrongful inclusion directly dilute outcomes for the rural poor.
static.whyInNews: The West Bengal Chief Minister flagged about 12,000 'fake' housing beneficiaries and ordered recovery of funds along with probes into officials.
static.wayForward: Strengthen social audit and third-party verification, use Aadhaar-based de-duplication, publish beneficiary lists in the public domain, and fix accountability through time-bound departmental inquiries.
prelimsPointers: PMAY-Gramin was launched in 2016 under the Ministry of Rural Development; PMAY-Urban was launched in 2015.
Beneficiary identification for PMAY-G uses SECC 2011 data and the Awaas+ app.
static.mainsAngle: Leakages in welfare delivery defeat the purpose of affirmative state spending; evaluate how technology and social audit can improve beneficiary targeting and accountability.

stories.headline: WHO flags teen inactivity; ovarian cancer blood test; cardiologist on heart health
stories.summary: Three health stories converge on the theme of prevention. WHO data indicate that nearly 240 million adolescents worldwide report no active days in a week, with only about 14% meeting recommended physical activity levels and girls consistently less active than boys. Separately, research reported by The Conversation suggests that early molecular changes linked to high-grade serous ovarian cancer — the most common and fastest-growing form of ovarian cancer, which often begins in a fallopian tube — may leave a detectable trace in the blood, opening a possible route to earlier diagnosis. A cardiologist's first-person account in The Indian Express completes the set by listing everyday habits he gave up to lower his own heart risk. Together they underline how lifestyle, screening and preventive care now shape the global disease burden.
stories.whyItMatters: Health sits at the intersection of GS-II social justice and GS-III science and technology; adolescent inactivity and non-communicable disease prevention bear directly on India's disease burden, human capital and welfare spending.

perspectives.take: Frames the WHO findings as a global public-health and equity failure, foregrounding the gender gap in adolescent activity and the need for safe, accessible spaces.
Research explainer from an academic platform: unpacks the biology behind a new blood-based early-detection lead for high-grade serous ovarian cancer, cautious about clinical translation.
Lifestyle/opinion framing — a cardiologist's personal list of habits to drop; practical and reader-friendly, but anecdotal rather than peer-reviewed evidence.

static.topic: Public health within India's welfare architecture
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare & Rights (Health)
static.whatIsIt: India's welfare model blends rights-based laws (MGNREGA 2005, RTE 2009, NFSA 2013) with DBT-enabled schemes and a JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) delivery backbone. Health is delivered through Ayushman Bharat, which has an insurance arm (PM-JAY) and Health & Wellness Centres.
static.background: Ayushman Bharat was launched in 2018 with its two arms — PM-JAY for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation cover, and Health & Wellness Centres for comprehensive primary care. POSHAN Abhiyaan targets malnutrition. Article 15/16 and Indra Sawhney (1992) frame reservation policy, while the four labour codes consolidate 29 labour laws.
static.geography: Access to safe play spaces, parks and sports infrastructure varies sharply between urban and rural India and across income groups.
static.socioEconomic: Adolescent inactivity tracks gender, income and safety: girls, poorer households and unsafe neighbourhoods show the lowest activity levels, compounding future NCD risk and out-of-pocket health expenditure.
static.whyInNews: WHO reports that nearly 240 million adolescents worldwide have no active days in a week, prompting renewed attention to preventive health within welfare design.
static.wayForward: Embed physical activity and screening in school curricula, Anganwadi and Health & Wellness Centre outreach; audit welfare delivery for exclusion errors and shift from entitlement to capability.
prelimsPointers: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year.
Four labour codes consolidate 29 existing labour laws.
static.mainsAngle: Welfare exclusion errors, urban poverty, and the shift from entitlement to capability — examine whether India's health welfare architecture is prevention-oriented.

static.topic: Non-communicable diseases and preventive health
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Health, NCDs & Disease Burden
static.whatIsIt: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) — cardiovascular diseases, cancers, diabetes and chronic respiratory diseases — account for roughly seven in ten deaths worldwide. WHO's Global Action Plan on NCDs sets voluntary targets, including a relative reduction in physical inactivity and in premature NCD mortality.
static.background: The WHO Global Action Plan on NCDs (2013–2020, extended to 2030) set nine voluntary targets. India runs the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS) under the National Health Mission, and launched the Fit India Movement in 2019 to promote physical activity.
static.socioEconomic: NCDs push households into catastrophic out-of-pocket expenditure; late diagnosis of cancers such as ovarian cancer worsens survival and cost outcomes, making early detection a socio-economic as well as clinical priority.
static.whyInNews: WHO adolescent inactivity data, new research on a possible blood-based early signal for high-grade serous ovarian cancer, and a cardiologist's lifestyle commentary all point to prevention and early detection.
static.wayForward: Strengthen population-level screening at primary care, regulate tobacco, alcohol and ultra-processed food, and build activity-friendly urban design and school sports infrastructure.
keyTerms: WHO Global Action Plan on NCDs
prelimsPointers: WHO recommends at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily for those aged 5–17.
High-grade serous ovarian cancer is the most common ovarian cancer subtype and often originates in the fallopian tube.
static.mainsAngle: Physical inactivity is a silent driver of the NCD burden — examine its gender and socio-economic dimensions in India and suggest policy measures.

prelims: WHO recommends at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily for children and adolescents aged 5–17.

Non-communicable diseases account for roughly seven in ten deaths worldwide; India's response includes NPCDCS under the National Health Mission and the Fit India Movement (2019).
stories.mainsQuestion: Physical inactivity and late diagnosis are increasingly recognised as drivers of the non-communicable disease burden. Examine the socio-economic and gender dimensions of declining adolescent physical activity in India and suggest policy measures for a prevention-oriented health system.

stories.headline: Adani Green project cost revision: Opposition seeks JPC, independent inquiry
stories.summary: Opposition parties in Maharashtra have demanded a Joint Parliamentary Committee or an inquiry by an independent higher authority into the revision of project costs for an Adani Green renewable energy project in Satara district, alleging the lowered cost helped the developer avoid statutory obligations. Adani Green has rejected the allegations, stating that the project — referred to in its response as the Tarali project — is located on private, non-forest land and does not affect protected areas or a tiger corridor. The dispute turns on how project cost is declared and whether that declaration bears on the statutory obligations a developer must meet. No independent authority has yet concluded on the allegations, and the company's rebuttal remains its own position.
stories.whyItMatters: The row tests the credibility of India's environmental clearance regime and the accountability of large private infrastructure — a recurring overlap of GS-II (executive accountability, parliamentary oversight), GS-III (environment law, infrastructure investment) and prelims-linked clearance rules.

perspectives.take: Frames the issue as one of accountability, foregrounding the Maharashtra opposition's demand for a JPC and an inquiry by an independent higher authority into the cost revision; regional political lens.

Carries the company's rebuttal — that the project sits on private, non-forest land with no impact on protected areas or the tiger corridor; business-press framing centred on statutory obligations and investor confidence.

static.topic: Biodiversity, Wetlands & Conservation
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Biodiversity & Conservation
static.whatIsIt: India is one of 17 megadiverse countries. Key instruments are the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, the Biological Diversity Act 2002 and the Forest Conservation Act 1980, alongside the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) and its Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022).
static.background: The Ramsar Convention (1971) protects wetlands and India has 80+ Ramsar sites. Project Tiger (1973) and Project Elephant (1992) anchor species conservation, and the 30x30 target aims to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.
static.geography: The Western Ghats–Sri Lanka is one of India's four biodiversity hotspots; the Western Ghats also contain tiger corridors and protected areas, which makes siting disputes in this landscape sensitive.
static.socioEconomic: Conservation siting decisions interact with land rights under the Forest Rights Act, local livelihoods and the flow of industrial and infrastructure investment.
static.whyInNews: Allegations over a renewable project's declared cost and its implications for statutory obligations, with the company asserting the site is private, non-forest land away from protected areas and a tiger corridor.
static.wayForward: Strengthen disclosure of project cost and clearance thresholds, and ensure independent verification of claims about forest status and corridor impacts.
prelimsPointers: India's biodiversity hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats–Sri Lanka, Sundaland/Nicobar.
World Wetlands Day: 2 February.
static.mainsAngle: Balancing conservation with development and community rights (FRA); human-wildlife conflict management.

static.topic: Environmental Clearance and EIA
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Environmental Impact Assessment & Clearance
static.whatIsIt: Environmental clearance is a prior approval required for listed projects under the EIA Notification, 2006, issued under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. Projects are categorised 'A' (appraised by the Centre's Expert Appraisal Committee) or 'B' (State Level Environment Impact Assessment Authority).
static.background: EIA was first made mandatory for certain projects in 1994 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; the current framework is the EIA Notification, 2006, amended several times since.
static.socioEconomic: Clearance conditions shape project costs, timelines and local environmental outcomes; disputes often turn on land classification (forest versus private) and proximity to protected areas or wildlife corridors.
static.whyInNews: Opposition parties allege that revising a project's declared cost downwards could affect the statutory obligations that apply; the company denies this and says the site is private, non-forest land.
static.wayForward: Transparent, publicly verifiable disclosures on cost and land status, plus credible independent appraisal, to preserve trust in the clearance regime.
prelimsPointers: The EIA Notification was issued in 2006 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
Category 'A' projects are appraised at the central level; Category 'B' projects at the state level.
static.mainsAngle: Effectiveness of the EIA regime in ensuring environmental accountability of large infrastructure projects.

static.topic: Parliamentary Committees and the JPC
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament: Committees and Accountability
static.whatIsIt: Departmentally Related Standing Committees function under the Rules of Procedure. A Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) is an ad hoc body that can be constituted by a motion in either House, with members drawn from both Houses, to investigate a specific subject.
static.background: JPCs have examined matters such as the Bofors deal (1987), the stock market scam (2001), the 2G spectrum issue (2011) and the Citizenship (Amendment) Bill (2019).
static.whyInNews: Opposition parties have demanded a JPC or an inquiry by an independent higher authority into the project cost revision.
static.wayForward: Use existing committee and audit mechanisms such as the Public Accounts Committee and the CAG for evidence-based scrutiny, while avoiding procedural gridlock.
prelimsPointers: A JPC is an ad hoc committee and can be constituted by a motion in either House of Parliament.
Departmentally Related Standing Committees were introduced in 1993.
static.mainsAngle: Role of parliamentary committees in ensuring executive accountability and transparency in large public-private projects.

stories.headline: World Bank backs AI-DPI push for SMEs; ORF flags port bunkering
stories.summary: World Bank executive director Neelkanth Mishra said India's small and medium business class could be transformed by a combination of never-before-cheap capital and technology built around artificial intelligence and Aadhaar-based digital public infrastructure. In a separate intervention, ORF argued that port bunkering — the supply of fuel to ships — represents India's next maritime advantage and an under-exploited services opportunity. Read together, both point to a common theme: India's next growth dividend may come less from building entirely new systems than from monetising and deepening the public assets it already has, digital and physical. The two also sit at different ends of the policy chain — one about credit and productivity for firms, the other about ports, logistics and the blue economy.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-II e-governance and data governance, and GS-III infrastructure, ports and industrial growth — DPI-plus-AI as an MSME credit enabler and port-led development as a logistics competitiveness lever are recurring UPSC themes.

perspectives.take: Frames DPI and AI as SME growth multipliers, with a World Bank economist stressing cheap capital and technology as twin enablers — a pro-market, reform-oriented business-press framing.

static.topic: Digital Public Infrastructure and SME Credit
static.syllabusNode: Governance — e-Governance & Data
static.whatIsIt: India's Digital Public Infrastructure — Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker — is a layered, interoperable stack. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs personal data processing.
static.background: Aadhaar (UIDAI, 2009) is the world's largest biometric ID. UPI (NPCI, 2016) processes billions of monthly transactions. The DPDP Act introduces a Data Protection Board and consent-based processing.
static.socioEconomic: DPI lowers transaction and verification costs, enabling credit flow to small businesses through account aggregators and digital lending; layering AI on this stack can improve underwriting and productivity for SMEs.
static.whyInNews: World Bank executive director Neelkanth Mishra cited AI and Aadhaar-based DPI as a potential game-changer for India's small and medium business class.
static.wayForward: Extend DPI into credit, health and logistics use cases, scale responsible AI adoption, and strengthen DPDP implementation and data-protection safeguards in parallel.
prelimsPointers: NPCI operates UPI, RuPay, IMPS and NACH.
The DPDP Act provides for consent, data-principal rights and significant data fiduciaries.
static.mainsAngle: Balance innovation with privacy and state surveillance; examine DPI as a global export model and as an enabler of MSME credit.

static.topic: Port Bunkering and Maritime Services
static.syllabusNode: Infrastructure — Ports & Shipping
static.whatIsIt: Bunkering is the supply of fuel — fuel oil, marine diesel or LNG — to ships at port. It is a high-value maritime service and a significant revenue stream for port economies.
static.background: Global bunkering is dominated by hubs such as Singapore, Rotterdam and Fujairah. India's Sagarmala programme (2015) and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways have pushed port-led development; the IMO's 2020 sulphur cap shifted demand towards cleaner marine fuels including LNG and methanol.
static.geography: India's long coastline and its major ports on both the western and eastern seaboards place it near key east-west shipping lanes, giving it natural bunkering potential.
static.socioEconomic: Bunkering generates port revenue, employment and ancillary services, and supports India's ambition to be a maritime logistics hub.
static.whyInNews: ORF argued that port bunkering is India's next maritime advantage.
static.wayForward: Build bunkering infrastructure and competitive pricing, and develop cleaner-fuel capacity (LNG, green methanol) to capture a share of the global bunkering market.
prelimsPointers: Bunkering refers to supplying fuel to ships.
The IMO's 2020 sulphur cap limited the sulphur content of marine fuels to 0.50% m/m.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how port-led development and maritime services can strengthen India's logistics competitiveness and blue economy.

static.topic: Multilateral Institutions and Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. The World Bank Group, a Bretton Woods institution, is a key multilateral development lender.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion of the Security Council; the Intergovernmental Negotiations remain inconclusive. India has also pressed for reform of multilateral development banks to expand development and climate finance.
static.socioEconomic: Multilateral lending shapes the capital available to developing economies; reform debates centre on voting weights, lending capacity and the terms on which finance reaches countries like India.
static.whyInNews: A World Bank executive director's remarks on India's capital and technology prospects spotlight the institution's role in shaping developing-country growth narratives.
static.wayForward: Continue pushing for UNSC expansion and for MDB reform that reflects current economic weights and expands concessional and climate finance.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for two-year terms.
The ICJ sits at The Hague; UN headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim to permanent UNSC membership rests on representativeness, population and contributions; assess the obstacles, including veto politics and the Ezulwini Consensus.

stories.headline: Norway press bodies question India visa move against journalist over Modi criticism
stories.summary: Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng Svendsen has said the Indian embassy in Oslo asked her to come in and return her visa, as reported by Telegraph India. The episode follows her critical reporting on Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Norwegian press bodies have publicly asked whether the visa action was retaliation for that criticism. Scroll.in reported that the media associations called the denial of entry to a journalist for asking critical questions a serious infringement of press freedom. On the available record, Indian authorities have not confirmed the reason for the visa action, and the row has renewed attention on how states deploy immigration powers against foreign correspondents.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the balance between a state's sovereign control over visas and the freedom of the press, and feeds into GS-II questions on fundamental rights, media freedom and India's international image.

perspectives.take: Frames the story through the journalist's own account — that the Indian embassy in Oslo summoned her and asked her to return her visa.
Frames it as a press-freedom question, foregrounding Norwegian media associations' demand to know whether the visa was revoked over criticism of PM Modi.

static.topic: Freedom of the Press in India
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Fundamental Rights (Article 19)
static.whatIsIt: Press freedom is not separately enumerated in the Constitution; it is read into Article 19(1)(a) as part of the freedom of speech and expression, and is subject to the reasonable restrictions listed in Article 19(2).
static.background: Early Supreme Court rulings such as Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950) and Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950) held that freedom of speech and expression includes the freedom to circulate and struck down prior restraint on publication. The Press Council of India, a statutory body, was first set up under the Press Council Act, 1965 and reconstituted under the Press Council Act, 1978 to safeguard the freedom of the press.
static.whyInNews: Norwegian press bodies have alleged that a visa action against a journalist critical of the Prime Minister amounts to an infringement of press freedom.
static.wayForward: Transparent, reasoned and consistently applied criteria for journalist visas, with clear communication of grounds, would reduce the scope for allegations of arbitrary action while preserving the state's legitimate security and foreign-policy concerns.
prelimsPointers: Press freedom in India flows from Article 19(1)(a) and is not a separate fundamental right.

Article 19(2) permits restrictions on grounds including sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether the constitutional guarantee of free expression adequately protects the press in an era of executive discretion over accreditation, access and the movement of foreign correspondents.

static.topic: Visa Policy and Regulation of Foreign Nationals
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Government Policies and Interventions; India and the World
static.whatIsIt: The entry, stay and exit of foreign nationals in India are regulated principally by the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920 and the Foreigners Act, 1946, while visas are issued by Indian missions abroad under the Ministry of External Affairs, including through the e-Visa route.
static.background: India's visa regime has been progressively liberalised since the 2014 introduction and later expansion of the e-Visa facility, with separate categories such as tourist, business, employment, student and journalist visas. Grant of a visa remains a sovereign act; a foreign national has no enforceable right to be admitted, and visas can be revoked or cancelled.
static.geography: Visa applications from Norway are processed through the Indian Embassy in Oslo.
static.whyInNews: A Norwegian journalist has said she was asked by the Indian embassy in Oslo to return her visa, prompting questions about the grounds for the action.
static.wayForward: Publishing clear, category-wise criteria and reasons for visa refusal or revocation would improve predictability for journalists, researchers and businesses without diluting sovereign discretion.
prelimsPointers: Visas to foreign nationals are issued by Indian missions abroad under the Ministry of External Affairs.
The Foreigners Act, 1946 governs the entry, presence and departure of foreigners in India.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the tension between the sovereign prerogative to regulate the entry of foreigners and the international norms protecting the movement of journalists and the free flow of information.

static.topic: India–Norway Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral, Regional and Global Groupings
static.whatIsIt: India and Norway maintain diplomatic relations covering trade and investment, renewable energy, the ocean economy, climate and Arctic affairs, alongside people-to-people and cultural links.
static.background: Norway has historically engaged with South Asia, including facilitating the 2002 Sri Lanka ceasefire process. Norway's Government Pension Fund Global is among the largest foreign institutional investors in Indian equity markets, and the two countries cooperate on energy transition, blue economy and environmental sustainability. India has an Arctic Policy and is an observer in the Arctic Council.
static.geography: Norway is a Nordic country in Northern Europe with its capital at Oslo; it is not a member of the European Union.
static.socioEconomic: Bilateral economic ties are anchored in Norwegian sovereign fund investments in Indian markets and cooperation in shipping, marine and renewable energy sectors.
static.whyInNews: A visa dispute involving a Norwegian journalist has brought the bilateral relationship into the news.
static.wayForward: Keeping people-to-people and media exchanges insulated from political friction would help preserve the broader economic and strategic partnership.
prelimsPointers: India is an observer in the Arctic Council.
Norway is not a member of the European Union and its capital is Oslo.
static.mainsAngle: Assess how visa and press-freedom controversies can affect India's bilateral ties with small but economically significant European partners.

prelims: Press freedom in India is derived from Article 19(1)(a) and is subject to the reasonable restrictions enumerated in Article 19(2).
Entry and stay of foreigners in India are governed principally by the Foreigners Act, 1946 and the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920.
Visas to foreign nationals are issued by Indian missions abroad under the Ministry of External Affairs, and their grant is a sovereign prerogative rather than an enforceable right.
Norway's capital is Oslo; India is an observer in the Arctic Council.

onThisDay.description: Labour MP Tam Dalyell raised what became known as the West Lothian question during a Commons debate on devolution. It asks why Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish MPs can vote on England-only matters while English MPs cannot vote on devolved matters.

onThisDay.title: Mariner 9 enters Mars orbit
onThisDay.description: NASA’s Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to enter orbit around another planet, Mars. It later mapped most of the Martian surface and provided key data for future Mars missions.
